rv.q: It's the most exhilarating example of locomotive storytelling on Broadway since the Royal Shakespeare Company's "Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby" visited three decades ago, with a cast that included a young actor named Roger Rees.
And you can be sure: Peter soars—deliriously high and gloriously far.
But in scaling up from a theater seating less than 200 to one with a capacity of around 1,000, the show’s larkish pantomime spirit has become strained.
It's supposed to connect with kids and adults alike, but ends up shortchanging both with a frantic, indulgent mess.
I'm happy to report that "Peter" has not given up a speck of its fairy dust–infused whimsy.

Alex Timbers and Roger Rees' spirited production of Rick Elice's play is that rare kind of theatrical event that can appeal equally to kids — who will be captivated by the sentimental, action-packed plot — and adults — who will admire its imaginative theatricality.
Adults will enjoy its complex theatricality... Kids will follow it for its bizarre and hammy characters and its constant sense of adventure.

This unusual tale of the origins of Peter Pan is winningly acted and inventively staged. The winning company who brought Rick Elice's Peter and the Starcatcher to life Off-Broadway at New York Theatre Workshop last year have now landed on Broadway at the Brooks Atkinson Theatre .

The comedy varies ("You like me! You really, really like me!" Ugh) and the switch to total earnestness at the end doesn't fly, but in digging into the roots of a familiar tale, Peter catches enough stardust, especially when it's at its most wicked.
And there are laughs aplenty  largely owing to Christian Borle’s turn as bombastic buccaneer Black Stache.
But 'Peter and the Starcatcher' just can't stop crowing about how clever it is.
This is a theater classic every bit as much as “Peter Pan” was.
Under the swift and farcical direction of Roger Rees and Alex Timbers, the company glows like starstuff itself.
Some of that charm is missing, unfortunately, from the Broadway version of the show, which opened on Sunday at the Brooks Atkinson Theatre.
“Peter and the Starcatcher” is also still, for my taste, too long and busy for what it is; it is still a struggle to stay engaged throughout.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this imaginative Peter Pan prequel for its inventive staging and stellar ensemble cast. A few find the Broadway transfer loses some Off-Broadway intimacy, but most agree it delivers clever, joyful theatrical magic.

vs.sum: The Lena Horne Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, with clear views even from the rear mezzanine. The sound quality is well-balanced across the theater. However, the seating is quite tight, especially for taller patrons, which affects comfort. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic architecture and restored interior, providing a charming atmosphere.

acc.note: Step-free entry and Orchestra. 5 wheelchair seats. No elevators.
